title: Is a custom LoRA trained on your own creatures enough to make AI creature generation ethical?
author: Savage_PrawnYT
selftext:
I’m a solo developer working on a monster-collecting RPG, and I recently had a debate on Reddit that made me think seriously about where people draw the ethical line with generative AI in games.

The criticism was basically: using generative AI for creature design is lazy, soulless, and built on stolen labour because models like Stable Diffusion were trained on large datasets that likely include copyrighted art and franchise creatures.

I understand that criticism. I don’t think it’s an unreasonable concern.

But the conversation became interesting when the other person suggested that a more ethical version would be to run the pipeline locally and train it on my own original monster designs, so the output is based on my own creative direction rather than just prompting for something like “Pokémon-style creature.”

My pipeline uses a custom LoRA trained on my own original creature designs. The goal is not to copy Pokémon or any specific artist, but to generate new creatures that belong to the visual/design language of my own game. I also curate the outputs, integrate them into Unity, build the battle systems, new element types, UI, world, quests, progression, and the actual game around them. It is not a one-click asset flip.

However, the LoRA still runs on top of Stable Diffusion 1.5, which itself was trained on a massive dataset. So even though I’m adding my own training layer and using my own source material, I can’t honestly claim the foundation model is completely isolated from the broader ethical concerns around scraped training data.

So I’m genuinely curious where people here draw the line.

Is using a custom LoRA trained on your own original creatures enough to make generative AI use ethically acceptable in a game?

Or is the foundation model itself still morally disqualifying, even if the developer is using their own dataset, running locally, being transparent, and building a full authored game around the pipeline?

For context, my game is here: https://store.steampowered.com/app/4701360/World\_of\_Qreatures/

For clarity, the reason I’m using generative AI is not simply to avoid drawing a fixed roster of monsters. The core mechanic of the game is that creatures can be generated at runtime, discovered through gameplay, evolved, and bred with other creatures to create new offspring. In other words, the AI system is part of the game design itself, not an asset-production shortcut.

I could use only the original monsters I created for the LoRA and build a traditional fixed roster, but then the game would be limited to a few hundred authored creatures. The concept I’m exploring is closer to genuinely open-ended creature generation, where players can discover and breed monsters that were not manually pre-designed in advance. That is the specific design problem the technology is being used to solve.

I’d really value honest opinions. I’m trying to use the technology as responsibly as I can, but I also realise different people have very different moral thresholds for this.

replies.author: Savage_PrawnYT
replies.body:
I built a locally run pipeline that uses a combination of various open source AI models that handle different things like image gen, image to 3D, audio gen for the monster cries, 3d to animated 3d for monster idle poses and stuff. The pipeline also includes my own custom Python modules for orchestration , monster stats and data and handling different routes that the pipeline can take such as standard generation or evolving or breeding to existing monsters together to create a new species. If you google open source image to 3D models, you will find lots of different models out there. In fact, I probably need to do a new search because there’s probably much better versions available now. I do actually have a patent pending for my particular implementation methods so I can’t go into too much detail.

The monsters for wild encounters and NPC trainer battles I have generated on my computer and move them into Unity manually. But for monsters that can be evolved bread or just generated from things like scanning real world QR code or for people that can’t scan QR codes they can. Enter a seed number in game and generate a new monster that way instead. For all of those actions it’s done at runtime. It takes about 90 seconds and the monster is sent to the players monster inventory whilst they are continuing to play the game such as catching monsters or exploring. This is essentially the exact pipeline I have running locally on my computer except it’s hosted on cloud service so all the heavy lifting is done in the cloud instead of on the users computer.

comments.author: lingotionny
comments.body:
Ethical AI is a multilayered issue. First, there is the abstract question of whether or not AI trained on scraped data is morally okay. Since the line there is different for everybody all we can say for sure is that your LoRA approach is better than pure stable diffusion, but not as good as training your own foundation model from scratch.

But setting that aside and going off of what other people have alluded to, the next question is if it is legally okay or constitutes copyright infringement. The US has the concept of fair use, but that is not the case for Europe and many other places. Even so, what is or is not fair use is still not fully clear, which means if you use output of a model trained on scraped data you are putting yourself at risk of copyright infringement. Anthropic found that out the hard way and settled for $1.5 billion in a class action.

But were are not done yet! Even if you do get by without infringement, there is then the matter of securing your own copyright on the output. And here the law has been pretty clear. AI cannot have copyright. This means the only chance for you to get copyright of the model's output is if you already have copyright of the training data and then argue that the model is not transformative but rather derivative of its training data, meaning the original training data copyright carries through to its output.

The only way to fully cover all three of these is to _only_ use your own or clearly licensed data and keep compliance documentation for when people come asking.

replies.author: lingotionny
replies.body:
It really is! What's kinda funny about copyright is that the arguments are completely opposing. Anthropic and others on the defence try to argue that their output does not infringe precisely because the model is transformative and that any copyright on the input is irrelevant because the output is too mangled. But even if that argument holds, that immediately disqualifies the case for holding copyright on the output since AI can't create new copyright.

Anthropic likely don't care about holding copyright but their users likely do. If you write a book, or other literary works using an llm then legally you have no protection and anyone can yoink your book. Same goes for generated assets and audio where the source model is trained on scraped data.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
Regarding books or images, copyright could come into play once you sufficiently edit those works manually. There is a difference between letting AI fully generate something and using it is a tool in a pipeline.

Specifically in game dev, unedited AI generated assets are borderline useless if you expect the game have any sort of commercial success.

replies.author: lingotionny
replies.body:
Valid point! There is definitely a point where manual work warrants a new copyright and then you would be the artist and copyright holder of the newly made piece. Exactly where that line is drawn is still fuzzy and I doubt you could take a genAI asset, manually polish a few details and pass it as your own, the same way you can't just take someone else's asset, edit a little and claim it as your own. Once again it becomes a question of whether your edit is transformative or derivative. (disclaimer: I do have some experience in the matter but since genAI and copyright is still legally fuzzy, we are in speculation territory so don't take my word for it)

In the case of this game, I understand the assets would be real time generated based on player actions (a very cool concept I might add) which means there is no chance to manually edit. Then there would probably be copyright issues.

replies.author: DocHolidayPhD
replies.body:
You are using a custom model. Custom models are unique. The model you are using is your own model. 

You are training the model on your own IP. Arguments stating that you could be ethically in the wrong for stealing art are therefore nullified. Arguments that you are making derivative works are therefore nullified.

The areas of contention are in the power and water usage that goes into the use of these algorithms and their training and the value of the returnable output. But these arguments are often on a case by case situation. If you spend a lot of energy and water training the model only to do nothing with it, it may be considered a waste. However, did you learn something by doing it? Was this worth it to you? If you wind up saving a bunch of production costs or time, then it's a clear benefit to you and potentially others should you make it available for others to use.

The blanket idea that AI is bad is absolute insanity. Few things in this world are uniformly good or evil. People have forgotten how to employ critical thinking in 2026.
